abstract: Sustainable utilization of aquaculture byproducts is imperative for advancing circular bioeconomy in food systems. This study developed an integrated in silico - in vitro screening strategy to identify novel angiotensin-converting enzyme (ACE) inhibitory peptides from grass carp swim bladder hydrolysates. Two novel peptides, FPSPFR (749.86 Da) and LWDPPEGAP (981.06 Da), were screened with IC 50 values of 81.34 μM and 206.91 μM, respectively. Kinetic characterization revealed non-competitive inhibition alongside exceptional gastrointestinal stability. Molecular docking showed strong binding affinities (−10.0 and −9.8 kcal/mol) via hydrogen bonding and hydrophobic interactions, while molecular dynamics simulations confirmed stable binding conformations. Network pharmacology and docking analysis suggested FPSPFR's potential antihypertensive effects through interactions with core targets including ALB, AKT1, SRC, ACE, MMP9 and STAT3. These results validate in silico analysis combined with in vitro assessments as an effective strategy for ACE inhibitory peptides discovery. Swim bladder-derived peptides demonstrated potent antihypertensive effects while enabling sustainable valorization of underutilized fishery processing byproducts, offering a viable pathway for functional food development and pharmaceutical applications.

Materials
Grass carp swim bladder collagen was extracted in accordance with the methods of
Dong and Dai (2022)
. Alcalase (from
Bacillus licheniformis

2.2
Enzymatic hydrolysis of swim bladder collagen
The swim bladder collagen was dissolved in Milli-Q water at 45 °C to prepare a 2 % substrate solution. The proteases were added at an enzyme-to-substrate ratio of 5000 U/g. The pH and temperature of the hydrolysis system. The optimum pH and hydrolysis temperature of the five proteases were set as follows: Papain (pH 7.0, 50 °C), Protamex (pH 7.0, 45 °C), Flavourzyme (pH 7.0, 50 °C), Neutrase (pH 7.0, 45 °C), and Alcalase (pH 9.0, 50 °C). After 3 h of enzymatic hydrolysis, the hydrolysates were treated at 90 °C for 10 min to inactivate the protease. The resulting mixture was then centrifuged, and the supernatant was freeze-dried to obtain swim bladder collagen hydrolysates powder (SBCH).
2.3
Peptide profile analysis
SBCH was separated using the EASY-nLC 1200 HPLC system (Thermo Fisher Scientific). Mobile phase A: formic acid (0.1 %), mobile phase B: formic acid (0.1 %)-80 % acetonitrile. The chromatographic column used was Acclaim PepMapTM RSLC (50 μm × 150 mm), equilibrated with 92 % buffer A. The gradient was programmed as follows: 8 % to 28 % buffer B over 98 min, 28 % to 37 % buffer B over 5 min, 37 % to 100 % buffer B over 5 min, and 100 % buffer B maintained for 3 min. The separated SBCH was analyzed using the Q Exactive HF-X Orbitrap mass spectrometer (Thermo Fisher Scientific) in positive ion mode. The selected mass range was 400–1800
m
/
z
, with a collision energy of 28 eV, a primary resolution of 60,000, and a secondary resolution of 15,000. Data acquisition was followed by identification and quantitation analysis using Proteome Discoverer 2.5, the protein sequence database employed corresponded to uniprot-TaxID 7959. The peptide mass tolerance was set to 10 ppm, and the fragment mass tolerance was set to 0.02 Da. The false discovery rate (FDR) threshold for peptides was established at 0.05.

2.8
Exploration of hypertension-related target identification
Hypertension-related genes were identified using Gene Cards, TTD, OMIM, Pharmgkb, and Drug Bank by searching the term “hypertension”. Genes retrieved from the Gene Cards database were sorted by relevance, and only those with a relevance score greater than 2 were selected. Genes obtained from the five databases were consolidated, duplicates were removed, and the union was taken to establish a repository of hypertension-related target genes. Potential target genes for FPSPFR and LWDPPEGAP were predicted using the Similarity Ensemble Approach (SEA), SwissTargetPrediction, and PharmMapper databases. After correcting and removing duplicates, the union of these gene sets was determined. The intersection between the hypertension-related genes and potential target genes was identified using a Venn diagram. Protein-protein interaction (PPI) network analysis was then conducted using Cytoscape 3.9.1.

body:
1
Introduction
Hypertension, a global health burden affecting over 1.6 billion individuals (
Chen, Wang, et al., 2021
), constitutes a principal etiological factor in cardiovascular and cerebrovascular diseases. Current pharmacological interventions targeting the renin-angiotensin system (RAS), particularly synthetic angiotensin-converting enzyme (ACE) inhibitors such as captopril and lisinopril, facing significant clinical limitations (
Khurana & Goswami, 2022
). Despite their efficacy in blood pressure regulation, these pharmaceuticals are frequently associated with dose-dependent adverse effects ranging from dry cough and angioedema to severe taste disturbances (
Fan et al., 2022
), necessitating the development of safer therapeutic alternatives.
Food-derived ACE-inhibitory peptides have garnered increasing attention due to their favorable safety profiles, reduced side effects, and enhanced bioavailability compared to synthetic counterparts. These bioactive oligopeptides, typically 2 to 20 amino acids, generated through controlled enzymatic hydrolysis exhibit antihypertensive effects through competitive or non-competitive inhibitions with ACE catalytic domains (
Rivero-Pino, 2023
). Structural determinants governing peptide-ACE inhibition have been systematically characterized: (i) sequence-specific molecular weight constraints; (ii) C-terminal aromatic or cyclic imino acid (Pro/Hyp) residues; (iii) N-terminal hydrophobic or basic amino acid enrichment (
Dong et al., 2024
). Collagen are rich in Pro, Hyp, and Gly, with hydrophobic amino acids accounting for more than 30 % of the total composition. From the perspective of structure–activity relationships of ACE inhibitory peptides, collagen serves as a good precursor protein for generating potential ACE inhibitory peptides. Various effective ACE inhibitory peptides have been identified in collagen hydrolysate such as bovine collagen (
Fu et al., 2016
), fish skin (
Dong et al., 2024
), and fish scale (
Jena et al., 2025
). Collagen hydrolysates or peptides obtained from marine sources have been reported to exhibit stronger ACE inhibitory activity compared to those derived from bovine, porcine, and poultry origins (
Tawalbeh et al., 2025
). Despite their potential, traditional methods for bioactive peptides screening remain labor-intensive, involving multiple steps such as protein hydrolysis, bioactivity assays, chromatographic fractionation, and structural identification (
Alavi & Ciftci, 2023
). Current estimates suggest over 90 % of potentially active sequences are lost during conventional purification processes, impeding structure-activity relationships characterization (
Fu et al., 2019
). Recent breakthroughs in high-throughput mass spectrometry, computational technologies and bioinformatics have revolutionized this field, enabling systematic identification of bioactive sequences from complex hydrolysates through
in silico
-
in vitro
integrated approaches (
Yu et al., 2023
).
Grass carp (
Ctenopharyngodon idella
) is a commonly cultivated freshwater fish species in China, with a total production exceeding 5.94 million tons in 2023, yielding 2.4 million tons of protein-rich byproducts (
Peng et al., 2025
). Although fish skin collagen has been widely studied for ACE inhibitory peptides extraction, swim bladders collagen remains underutilized despite its biochemical potential. Compared to fish skin and scales, swim bladders contain lower amounts of heterologous proteins and glycosaminoglycans, making the collagen extraction process relatively simpler (
Han et al., 2025
). Current research on swim bladder-derived ACE inhibitory peptides includes miiuy croaker (
Miichthys miiuy
) collagen peptides SHGEY and SPYGF (
Zhu et al., 2022
), as well as monkfish-originated SEGPK, FDGPY and SPGPW (
Hu et al., 2023
), have been isolated from swim bladder. However, these ACE inhibitory peptides exhibit significantly lower potency compared to skin-derived analogues such as VGLFPSRSF (
Dong et al., 2024
). This efficacy gap, combined with limited understanding of critical structure-activity relationships and multi-target interactions within cardiovascular pathways, currently hinders the development of clinically viable ACE inhibitors from swim bladder collagen.
This study integrated computational and experimental approaches to systematically identify novel ACE-inhibitory peptides from grass carp swim bladder collagen hydrolysates. Through molecular docking, dynamics simulations, and network pharmacology analyses, we elucidated the structural basis of peptide-ACE interactions and their multi-target regulatory effects on hypertension-related pathways. Our findings advance the development of natural ACE inhibitors while establishing a sustainable strategy for high-value utilization of fishery byproducts.

3
Results and discussion
3.1
Preparation of the SBCH
Fig. 1
A illustrates the ACE inhibitory activity of SBCH prepared
via
five commercial proteases. SBCH prepared using exhibited superior ACE inhibitory activity, with an ACE inhibition rate of 56.59 % (1 mg/mL) and an IC
50
of 0.79 mg/mL, which was significantly higher than that of the fish collagen protein hydrolysates (45.54 %, 1.67 mg/mL) (
Yu et al., 2020
), and Monkfish swim bladder collagen hydrolysate prepared by dual enzyme (Alcalase + Neutrase) hydrolysis systems (
Hu et al., 2023
). It indicated that SBCH can serve as a valuable source of natural ACE inhibitory peptides. The hydrolysates prepared using Protamex appear to be rich reservoirs of potential ACE inhibitors, and thus Protamex hydrolysate was selected for further investigation.

3.2
Peptide profile analysis
LC-MS/MS analysis identified 535 peptides in SBCH (
Fig. 1
B), with oligopeptides constituting over 50 % of the total (
Fig. 1
C). Among these peptides, hexapeptides were notably the most abundant in SBCH. Previous studies have indicated that short peptides displayed superior ACE inhibitory activity through reduced steric hindrance and enhanced binding efficiency (
Lin et al., 2018
). The high proportion of low molecular weight peptides in SBCH might contribute to enhancing its bioactivity.
Further analysis was conducted on the peptide's amino acid distribution within SBCH (
Fig. 1
D). Notably, amino acid composition analysis revealed enrichment of Gly, Pro, Leu and Val in SBCH peptide. The peptide composition in SBCH exhibited a higher proportion of Ile, Leu, Val, Pro, and Gly at the N-terminal and an elevated proportion of Pro, Phe, Leu, Ala, and Gly at the C-terminal. Previous research has demonstrated that peptides containing hydrophobic or basic amino acids at the N-terminal position tend to exhibit heightened ACE inhibitory activity. Furthermore, peptides with aromatic amino acids and proline at the C-terminal display enhanced ACE inhibitory activity (
Zhang et al., 2013
). Hydrophobic amino acids (
e.g.
, Phe, Leu, and Pro) have been shown to facilitate stronger binding of peptides to the ACE (
Yin et al., 2022
). In addition, the pyrrole ring within proline plays a crucial role in ACE inhibition, and its presence in peptides enhances their stability during digestion in the gastrointestinal tract (
Chen, Sun, et al., 2021
). The high content of hydrophobic terminals combined with conformationally rigid Pro residues, provide a mechanistic rationale for SBCH's potent ACE inhibitory activity while highlighting its viability as a bioactive peptide source.
3.3
In silico screening of potential ACE inhibitory peptides
To identify high-potential bioactive peptides from SBCH, we implemented a multi-step
in silico
screening strategy. Initial bioactivity prediction using PeptideRanker (threshold: 0.65) identified 143 candidate peptides, significantly exceeding the conventional 0.5 threshold (
Garzón et al., 2022
), to minimize false negatives . Subsequent water solubility prediction
via
Innovagen's platform narrowed this pool to 65 soluble peptides, a critical determinant for oral bioavailability. The physicochemical properties of these 65 water-soluble peptides were further analyzed, including toxicity, allergenicity, isoelectric point (pI), molecular weight, and net charge at pH 7.0 (
Table 1
). Among them, 17 basic (with 15 of them exhibiting a net charge of 1 at pH 7.0), 46 acidic, and 2 neutral pI values. Safety evaluation further identified 12 non-toxic and non-allergenic candidates, predominantly oligopeptides known for enhanced absorption (
Liu et al., 2021
). PASTA 2.0 structural analysis confirmed these peptides consistently exhibited molecular stability and adopted stable random helical conformations without amyloid formation or self-aggregation tendencies, regardless of individual hydrophobicity (Table S2).

The assessment of ADMET profiles is imperative for the subsequent utilization of peptides as bioactive agents. ADMET evaluation was performed using admetSAR for the 12 peptides described above, evaluating blood-brain barrier penetration (BBB), human intestinal absorption (HIA), Caco-2 permeability, metabolic properties, toxicity, and potential skin sensitization for topical administration (
Table 2
). HIA is a crucial parameter for screening peptides with favorable gastrointestinal absorption. Peptides with an absorption rate exceeding 30 % are categorized as HIA+, while those below this threshold are labeled as HIA-. Additionally, CYP450 enzymes significantly affect the metabolism of a wide range of endogenous and exogenous compounds (
Liu et al., 2021
). The data suggested that these 12 peptides showed high Caco-2 permeability and showed no interaction with CYP450 enzymes. This suggests that the efficacy and safety of these peptides remain unaffected by CYP450 enzymes, indicating that they are non-substrates or non-inhibitors in metabolism. Furthermore, five HIA+ candidates, AINDPF, MDGSGF, GEPGLL, LWDPPEGAP and FPSPFR, underwent dual computational evaluation for antihypertensive potential through machine learning-driven prediction (mAHTPred) and structural homology alignment (AHTpin). The meta-predictor mAHTPred employs ensemble machine-learning algorithms integrating six classifiers (SVM, RF, GB, ERT, AdaBoost, k-nearest neighbor) to evaluate antihypertensive potential (
Manavalan et al., 2019
), while AHTpin's structural alignment analysis identified sequence homology with established ACE inhibitors (
Kumar et al., 2015
). According to the predicted results, AINDPF, LWDPPEGAP and FPSPFR were selected for experimental validation.

3.4
ACE inhibitory activity and inhibition kinetics
As shown in
Table 3
, FPSPFR and LWDPPEGAP exhibited potential ACE inhibition with IC
50
values of 81.34 and 206.91 μM, respectively, while AINDPF showed no ACE inhibitory activity (IC
50
> 1000 μM). These findings align with established structural patterns for potent ACE inhibitors: peptides containing C-terminal positively charged or aromatic amino acids (
e.g.
, Lys, Arg, Trp, Tyr, and Phe), and N-terminal hydrophobic amino acids (
e.g.
, Ile, Ala, Met, and Leu) typically exhibit enhanced activity (
Gao et al., 2021
). The critical role of terminal residues is further supported by documented ACE inhibitors like LTGCP (
Wang, Wang, et al., 2024
;
Wang, Zhang, et al., 2024
) and RFFGP (
Ren et al., 2023
), both featuring C-terminal proline, a residue known to promote binding at the enzyme's catalytic site along with Val, Ala, Leu and Ile (
Wang, Wang, et al., 2024
;
Wang, Zhang, et al., 2024
). Additionally, LWDPPEGAP and FPSPFR exhibited greater potency superior (lower IC
50
values) than marine-derived counterparts such as SEGPK (1220 μM), FDGPY (1573 μM) and SPGPW (1309 μM) from Monkfish swim bladders (
Hu et al., 2023
), SPYGF (649.6 μM) and SHGEY (1454 μM) from Miiuy croaker swim bladders (
Zhu et al., 2022
). According to
Panyayai et al. (2018)
, the IC
50
values of peptides between 0.32 and 1000 μM are considered as potential antihypertensive agents. The strong ACE inhibitory activity of FPSPFR and LWDPPEGAP highlights their promise as ACE inhibitors. This study reinforces the value of
in silico
screening strategies for efficiently identifying bioactive peptides with ACE inhibitory properties.

3.5
Gastrointestinal digestive stability
As shown in
Fig. 2
, FPSPFR and LWDPPEGAP retained their ACE inhibitory activity with no significant difference (
P
> 0.05) following exposure to pepsin and trypsin. This phenomenon may be attributed to two possible reasons. First, the presence of proline residues in peptides FPSPFR and LWDPPEGAP may confer enhanced stability during gastrointestinal digestion, as proline-containing peptides are generally more resistant to enzymatic hydrolysis due to the cyclic structure of proline (
Ashaolu et al., 2023
). For example, the heptapeptide SPAIPLP, which is rich in proline, exhibited good gastrointestinal stability (
Lin et al., 2024
). Second, FPSPFR and LWDPPEGAP might have been hydrolyzed into smaller peptide fragments that still retained ACE inhibitory activity. The smaller peptides generated during digestion, together with the undigested fragments, may exert a synergistic effect that preserves bioactivity (
Ye et al., 2025
).
Liang et al. (2024)
reported that the peptide IIVFGRQLL was cleaved into five fragments (IVF, IVFG, VF, FGR, and RQL) during simulated digestion, among which IVF, VF, and FGR retained ACE inhibitory activity. Similarly, the peptide KYPHVF was digested into YPHVF and PHVF, both of which exhibited stronger ACE inhibitory activity than the parent peptide, likely due to increased aromatic amino acid content (
Li et al., 2023
). PeptideCutter was used to predict the potential cleavage sites of pepsin and trypsin. The results indicated that FPSPFR may be degraded into FPSP, FR, and PSPFR, while peptide LWDPPEGAP may be degraded into WDPPEGAP. Furthermore, bioactivity predictions using mAHTPred and AHTpin suggested that these degradation products may still possess antihypertensive activity. It should be noted that the current assessment of gastrointestinal stability was based solely on changes in ACE inhibitory activity. The structural integrity of the peptides post-digestion has not yet been directly confirmed. Future studies are needed to analyze the specific composition of the digestion products using HPLC or mass spectrometry.
3.6
Molecular docking
Molecular docking is commonly used to elucidate the binding modes, binding sites, and affinities between peptides and ACE, thereby indicating their
in vitro
ACE inhibitory potential (
Bao et al., 2025
). As shown in Fig. S2, Captopril interacted with the active site residues of ACE with a binding energy of −6.3 kcal/mol. Specifically, it formed three hydrogen bonds with Tyr523, His513, and His353, two Pi-Alkyl interactions with Val380 and His383, and coordinated with Zn
2+
via
a metal-acceptor interaction. These findings were consistent with the report by
Phakeenuya and Wonganu (2025)
which indicated that captopril interacted with Gln281, His353, Lys511, His513, Tyr520, and Tyr523 with a binding energy of −5.9 kcal/mol. As shown in
Table 3
and
Fig. 4
, FPSPFR showed the lowest binding energy (−10.0 kcal/mol) among screened peptides. Negative binding energy indicates that the binding between the peptide and ACE is spontaneous, with lower binding energy reflecting a more stable interaction (
Lin et al., 2025
). The thermodynamic stability of FPSPFR-ACE complex correlated with its lower IC
50
values, consistent with the established relationship between binding energy and inhibitory potency. Antihypertensive peptides primarily inhibit ACE activity by interacting with it through hydrogen bonds, van der Waals forces, and electrostatic interactions (
Ye et al., 2025
). FPSPFR bound to ACE through hydrogen bonds (Glu 123, His 410, Gly 404, Glu 403 and Arg 522), Pi-alkyl interactions (Ala 89, Arg 124, Trp 59 and Ala 356), and Pi-sigma contact (Ile 88). Its Pi-cation attraction to the catalytic zinc ion (Zn 701) directly coordinated the metal center, a critical feature linked to enhanced inhibition potency (
Duan et al., 2023
). In contrast, LWDPPEGAP exhibited a divergent binding strategy: hydrogen bonds extend to His 387 and Pro 519, while broader Pi-alkyl interactions engaged residues across multiple domains (Ala 207, Ile 204, Tyr 62, Trp 357 and His 387). Notably, LWDPPEGAP uniquely exploited Pi-anion interactions with Glu 123, suggesting divergent ACE recognition strategies between the two peptides. The non-competitive inhibitory peptides FPSPFR and LWDPPEGAP did not interact with the active sites (S1, S2, and S′) of ACE, which is consistent with their kinetic results. Similar findings were reported by
Windarto et al. (2022)
and
Wei et al. (2024)
who found that the peptides VL-9 and FDRPFL, respectively, acted as non-competitive inhibitors by binding outside the ACE catalytic center and forming strong electrostatic or hydrogen-bond interactions with inactive site residues.
Fu et al. (2016)
demonstrated that the collagen peptides VGPV and GPRGF are non-competitive inhibitory peptides, as they neither occupy the S1 and S2 subsites of ACE nor compete with the substrate for the active site.
Du et al. (2024)
found that the non-competitive peptide ITAPHW does not interact with the active pocket (S1, S2, and S1′) of ACE, yet its IC
50
value is significantly lower than that of other peptides, which may be related to the interaction between ITAPHW and the Zn
2+
of ACE. The interaction between peptides and Zn
2+
is considered to play a crucial role in ACE inhibition, with Ala 356 and Arg 522 being reported as key active site residues (
Ye et al., 2025
). FPSPFR interacted with Ala356 and Arg522
via
hydrogen bonding and formed a Pi–cation interaction with Zn
2+
, participating in coordination at the metal center. This may explain why FPSPFR exhibited stronger ACE inhibitory activity than LWDPPEGAP.
3.7
Molecular dynamics simulations
To further characterize the dynamic stability of peptide-ACE complexes, molecular dynamics simulations were performed. System equilibrium was confirmed by RMSD analysis, with both ACE and its complexes (ACE-FPSPFR, ACE-LWDPPEGAP) reaching structural stability within 20 ns, followed by sustained conformational integrity throughout the simulation (
Fig. 2
D), which is consistent with the findings of
Lin et al. (2025)
. Structural integrity metrics further supported complex stabilization. The changes in the solvent-accessible surface area (SASA) can be used to predict structural variations in protein complexes upon ligand binding. Limited structural perturbations were evidenced by minimal SASA fluctuations (
Fig. 2
E). The radius of gyration (Rg) is defined as the average distance between the center of mass of all atoms and their terminal points over specific time intervals and evaluates the compactness of protein structure during the simulation. The consistent radius of gyration (Rg) profiles (
Fig. 2
F) indicated preserved protein compactness. Root-mean-square fluctuation (RMSF) analysis revealed marginal deviations across complexes (ACE: 0.0776 nm; ACE-FPSPFR, 0.0810 nm; ACE-LWDPPEGAP, 0.0767 nm;
Fig. 2
G), confirming that peptide binding did not compromise ACE's native structural stabilization. A robust hydrogen bonding network was maintained in ACE-FPSPFR (average 4.85 bonds for ACE-FPSPFR and 4.64 for ACE-LWDPPEGAP;
Fig. 2
H), suggesting enhanced binding affinity (
Lin et al., 2025
), in agreement with the molecular docking results and the
in vitro
activity measurements. Binding free energy calculations were performed using gmx_mmpbsa script (
https://jerkwin.github.io/gmxtool/
) to quantify protein-ligand interaction energy during the equilibrium phase. The ACE-FPSPFR complex demonstrated superior stablity with a binding free energies of −195.786 kJ/mol, nearly double that of ACE-LWDPPEGAP (−122.019 kJ/mol;
Table 4
). Therefore, FPSPFR exhibited stronger ACE inhibitory activity, which is consistent with the
in vitro
experimental results.

These computational insights align with experimental kinetics, where FPSPFR's 2.5-fold greater inhibitory potency correlates directly with its enhanced thermodynamic stability and optimized interaction profile. The persistent Zn
2+
coordination and non-competitive inhibition signature (
via
Ala 356 and Arg 522 engagement) further rationalize FPSPFR's mechanism, consistent with recent reports highlighting metal-ion interactions as critical determinants of ACE inhibition efficacy (
Ye et al., 2025
). Collectively, the MD-derived parameters, such as structural stability, energy landscapes, and dynamic interaction networks, provide a multiscale rationale for the functional divergence between these peptides.
3.8
Network pharmacology and multi-target analysis
To explore the potential multi-target antihypertensive potential of FPSPFR and LWDPPFR, we integrated network pharmacology analysis with molecular docking, a strategy increasingly used to map drug-gene-disease interactions through omics integration and computational modeling. Building on this approach, 1988 hypertension- associated genes (H_1988) were identified from database. Subsequent target prediction revealed 430 and 349 potential binding partners for FPSPFR (F_430) and LWDPPEGAP (L_349), respectively. Notably, 137 and 121 of these targets overlapped with H_1988 (
Fig. 3
A), suggesting direct relevance to hypertension pathophysiology. PPI network analysis further revealed conserved hub genes across both peptides, including ALB (a known ACE inhibitor modulating RAAS) (
Fagyas et al., 2014
), AKT1 (angiogenesis regulator) (
Heron-Milhavet et al., 2011
), MMP9 (cardiovascular remodeling mediator) (
Lindsey et al., 2006

Conclusion
This study identified 535 peptide sequences from grass carp swim bladder collagen hydrolysates, with over 50 % being oligopeptides. Through a combined
in silico
-
in vitro
strategy, FPSPFR and LWDPPEGAP were rapidly identified, exhibiting potent ACE inhibition with IC
50
values of 81.34 μM and 206.91 μM, respectively. Both peptides showed non-competitive inhibition patterns and maintained high gastrointestinal stability. Molecular docking revealed FPSPFR's strong binding to ACE
via
hydrogen bonding and hydrophobic interactions, while molecular dynamics simulations confirmed the structural stability of these interactions over time. Network pharmacology analysis suggested FPSPFR's potential in blood pressure regulation through interaction with core targets including ALB, AKT1, SRC, ACE, MMP9 and STAT3. These findings highlight grass carp swim bladder as a valuable source for ACE inhibitory peptides, validating the efficiency of structure-guided discovery route for bioactive peptide development. The superior activity and polypharmacological profile of FPSPFR underscore its potential as a multi-mechanistic antihypertensive agent. Future investigations should prioritize
in vivo
validation of its blood pressure-lowering efficacy and oral bioavailability to bridge computational predictions with therapeutic applications.
